claims.text: High-throughput combinatorial co-sputtering can fabricate composition-spread HfNbTaTiZr thin films.
Systematically varying individual elemental percentages in HfNbTaTiZr will produce measurable, spatially localized mechanical-property differences relative to an equiatomic composition.
The baseline is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr thin film.
An equiatomic HEA has equal proportions of its principal elements.
Co-sputtering can create a continuous HfNbTaTiZr compositional gradient away from the equiatomic ratio.
Nanoindentation and micro-compression can respectively provide localized hardness and yield-strength measurements across the gradient.
EDS can correlate local composition with mechanical properties, while TEM or XRD can characterize associated microstructure.
Non-equiatomic compositions will induce local differences in lattice distortion.
Non-equiatomic compositions may induce local grain-size differences.
Non-equiatomic compositions may induce minor phase changes.
Changing elemental percentages modifies the local lattice structure and lattice distortion.
Changes in local lattice structure and distortion affect dislocation mobility.
Changing elemental percentages alters the balance of strengthening mechanisms.
Lattice distortion and related HEA core effects contribute to hardness and strength.
Hf-enriched regions are expected to have increased hardness because Hf has a larger atomic radius.
Other compositional variations may increase or decrease yield strength relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Mechanical-property trends will be spatially resolved across the compositional gradient.
Equiatomic regions tested under identical conditions provide the control baseline.
The inferred effects are specific to thin films under ambient laboratory conditions and may not extrapolate to bulk materials or extreme environments.
A lack of systematic mechanical-property differences from the equiatomic control, or an absence of the predicted microstructural variations, would falsify the hypothesis.
